text: Can you help me plan the unpacking? There are boxes everywhere and I'm not sure where to start.

Sure. The trick is to unpack in the order you need things to live day to day, not room by room in whatever order the boxes landed. Here's a plan that works for most people:

Day 1: the survival layer
- Beds first. Assemble the frames, or at least get the mattresses down and make them up with clean sheets. A good night's sleep matters more than anything else this week.
- Bathroom basics: towels, toilet paper, soap, toothbrushes, a shower curtain, and any daily prescriptions.
- Dog setup: food and water bowls, food, leashes, poop bags, and their beds or blankets. Familiar-smelling bedding helps them feel at home faster.
- A few kitchen essentials: one pan, one pot, a knife, a cutting board, a couple of plates and bowls, mugs, and the coffee or tea setup.

Days 2 and 3: the kitchen
The kitchen has the most items and the most decisions, so give it a full block of time. Unpack in this order: everyday dishes and utensils, pantry staples, cookware, then small appliances. Leave rarely used items (serving platters, specialty gadgets, seasonal baking gear) in their boxes and stash those boxes in a closet to sort later.

Days 4 and 5: bedroom and clothes
Hang what you wear most, fold the rest, and don't worry about organizing drawers perfectly. Good enough is fine for now.

Week 2: living areas, books, decor, and any storage boxes.

A few tips that speed things up:
- Break down boxes as you empty them and stack them flat by the door. Visible progress is motivating, and it clears floor space.
- Keep one open 'misc' box per room for things that don't have a home yet, instead of letting them spread across counters.
- Work in 45-minute stretches with a 15-minute break. Long unbroken sessions lead to burnout by day three.
That helps. Can you expand the change-of-address list? I keep remembering places I forgot.

Here's a fuller list, grouped so you can work through it in one or two sittings. Most of these take a few minutes each online.

Official
- USPS mail forwarding, if it isn't set up yet. Forwarding can run up to a year, but update senders directly so you aren't relying on it.
- IRS: you can file Form 8822, or simply use the new address on your next return.
- Voter registration for Idaho.
- Any professional licenses or memberships that mail renewals.

Money
- Banks and credit unions
- Credit cards (the billing ZIP code is often used to verify card purchases, so update it early to avoid declined payments)
- Investment and retirement accounts
- Payment apps like PayPal or Venmo
- Any loan servicers

Insurance
- Health insurance (your plan's network may differ in a new state, so check that too)
- Renters or homeowners insurance
- Life insurance
- Pet insurance, if the dogs have it

Health
- Doctor and dentist (or request records to be sent to new ones)
- Pharmacy: transfer prescriptions to a local branch
- Eye doctor

Shopping and subscriptions
- Default shipping info on Amazon and other retailers. This is the one people forget most, and packages end up at the old place.
- Meal kits, subscription boxes, and pet food deliveries
- Streaming services and phone carrier (billing info)

The dogs
- Microchip registry. It's easy to overlook, and it's what a shelter uses to reach you if one of them gets loose.
- ID tags with a current phone number
- Vet records and the city dog license

A useful habit: over the next couple of months, glance at every piece of forwarded mail. Anything that arrives through forwarding is a sender you missed, so update it right then.
What should I look for when choosing a vet for the dogs?

Good thing to sort out before you need one. Here's what to weigh:

Practical basics
- Distance. Close enough that a quick visit is easy, since you'll be there more often than you expect.
- Hours. Ask whether they offer early morning, evening, or Saturday appointments.
- Emergency coverage. Ask what they do after hours. Most general clinics refer to a 24-hour emergency hospital, so find out which one and save its number in your phone now.
- Booking. How far out are routine appointments booked? Can you get a same-day sick visit?

Care and conversation
- Do the vets explain options and costs before treating, or just proceed?
- Do they send estimates in writing for anything beyond a routine exam?
- Is there a patient portal for records, reminders, and messaging?
- Are they open to questions about food, behavior, and preventive care, or do visits feel rushed?

Credentials and setup
- AAHA accreditation is a voluntary standard that covers things like anesthesia monitoring, sterilization, and record keeping. Not every good clinic has it, but it's a positive sign.
- Fear Free certified staff can make visits less stressful for anxious dogs.
- Ask whether they do dental cleanings, X-rays, and bloodwork in-house or send you elsewhere.

How to find candidates
- Ask neighbors you meet on walks. Dog owners on the Greenbelt are usually happy to share opinions.
- Read recent reviews, focusing on how the clinic handled problems rather than star ratings alone.
- Call two or three clinics and ask about new-patient availability and exam fees. How the front desk treats you on the phone tells you a lot.

Once you pick one, book a wellness visit for each dog while they're healthy. It sets a baseline, gets them into the system, and makes a future sick visit much faster to arrange.
How do I get their records sent over from the old vet?

It's usually quick. Here's the process:

1. Call or email the old clinic and ask for the complete medical records for each dog, not just the vaccine summary. Full records include exam notes, lab results, past prescriptions, and any surgeries or dental work.
2. Ask them to email the records as PDFs to you, and also send them straight to the new clinic once you've chosen one. Having your own copy means you're never stuck waiting on a fax.
3. Request proof of current rabies vaccination for each dog. Most cities, including Boise, ask for it when you license a dog, so you'll want it handy.
4. Write down each dog's microchip number and the registry company. It's often in the records, but double-check.
5. Note any prescriptions, doses, and refill dates so the new vet can take over prescriptions without a gap.

Store everything in one folder on your phone or in cloud storage, named clearly by dog. When the new clinic sends its intake form, you can attach the files and be done in a few minutes.

If the old clinic is slow, a polite follow-up after a few days usually does it. Clinics handle these requests constantly.
Any tips for helping dogs settle into a new home?

Yes, a few things make a real difference:

Keep the routine steady
Dogs take a lot of comfort from predictability. Feed them, walk them, and settle them for bed at the same times you always have. When the house is unfamiliar, the schedule becomes their anchor.

Set up their space first
Put their beds, bowls, and toys in spots that will stay put, so they learn where 'their' places are. Don't wash their bedding for the first week or two; the familiar smell is reassuring.

Explore gradually
Let them sniff the house room by room with you nearby. Close off any rooms with unpacked boxes, cords, or cleaning supplies until those areas are sorted.

Check the yard and doors
Walk the fence line, if there is one, and look for gaps or loose boards. In a new place, dogs are more likely to bolt if a door is left open, so be extra careful during the unpacking chaos when people are coming and going.

Burn off energy
Long sniffy walks are calming because sniffing is mentally tiring. The Greenbelt is ideal for that. A tired dog adapts faster.

Expect a little adjustment
Some dogs are restless at night, bark at new sounds, or have a small accident in the first week or two. That's normal. Stay calm, keep the routine, and it usually fades on its own. If anything persists past a few weeks, mention it at the first vet visit.

Update their tags
If it's not done yet, put a phone number on their collars today. It's the single most important safety step during a transition.
And for utilities and internet, anything I should double-check?

A few things worth confirming now so there are no surprises on the first bills:

- Start dates. Make sure each service is in your name starting on the day you took possession, and that the old place's accounts are closed so you're not paying for both.
- Providers. In Boise, electricity is generally Idaho Power and natural gas is usually Intermountain Gas. Water and trash can vary by neighborhood, so confirm who serves your home.
- Deposits. Some utilities waive the deposit if you have a good payment history or a letter of credit from your previous provider. It's worth asking.
- Trash and recycling. Find out your pickup day and what goes in which bin. Recycling rules differ a lot between cities, so check the current list rather than assuming.
- Internet. Confirm the speed you're actually getting with a quick speed test, and compare it to what you're paying for. If it's far lower, call support early while the install is fresh.
- Router placement. Put the router in a central, open spot, off the floor and away from the microwave. Change the default Wi-Fi name and password, and the router's admin password too.
- Autopay and paperless billing. Set these up once you've seen the first bill and know it's correct.
- Meter readings. Take photos of the meters on day one. If there's ever a billing dispute, you have a timestamped starting point.
Last one: a simple meal plan for this week while most of the kitchen is still in boxes?

Here's a low-effort plan that needs only one pan, one pot, and a sheet tray:

Breakfasts (rotate)
- Overnight oats in jars: oats, milk or yogurt, fruit. Make three at once.
- Toast with eggs or avocado.
- Yogurt, granola, and fruit when you're short on time.

Lunches
- Wraps with rotisserie chicken, greens, and hummus.
- Leftovers from the previous dinner.
- A big grain salad made on Sunday: cooked rice or farro, canned beans, chopped vegetables, olive oil, and lemon. It keeps for four days.

Dinners
- Night 1: sheet-pan sausage and vegetables. Toss everything with oil and salt, roast at 425°F for about 25 minutes.
- Night 2: pasta with jarred sauce, a bag of spinach stirred in, and parmesan.
- Night 3: tacos with rotisserie chicken or canned black beans, salsa, and shredded cabbage.
- Night 4: fried rice with frozen vegetables and eggs. Uses up leftover rice.
- Night 5: takeout. You've earned it, and it's a good way to try a local spot.
- Night 6: quesadillas and a bagged salad kit.
- Night 7: soup from a carton, upgraded with frozen dumplings or tortellini, and toast.

Shopping list basics
Rotisserie chicken, eggs, bread, tortillas, a carton of soup, pasta, jarred sauce, rice, canned beans, frozen vegetables, a bag of spinach, salad kit, cheese, salsa, hummus, yogurt, fruit, oats, olive oil, salt.

A couple of tips: use paper plates for the first few days if the dishwasher isn't hooked up yet, and keep a roll of foil on hand so the sheet tray needs almost no cleanup. Once the kitchen is unpacked, you can go back to cooking the way you like.
